question_bank.stem: A frontier lab wants a first health check on whether a model is training normally. Which signal does the lecture name as the natural starting point?

options.text: Loss curves following a smooth trajectory
A single public benchmark score
An occlusion heatmap over an input image
A generator output from a random code

question_bank.rationale: The instructor says a natural way to check training is to inspect loss curves and make sure they follow a smooth trajectory.

distractor_rationales.B: Benchmark scores evaluate capabilities, but the starting training-health signal here is the loss curve.
distractor_rationales.C: Occlusion heatmaps are CNN interpretability tools.
distractor_rationales.D: Generator outputs are not frontier-model training telemetry.

frame_evidence.description: Slide displays loss curves as a training-health diagnostic and examples of ugly or jumpy curves.

question_bank.stem: A sudden jump in the loss curve is treated as a diagnostic warning because it can indicate what issue?

options.text: Corrupted data, code bugs, or gradient problems
A correctly balanced MoE router
A successful class activation map
A fixed and uncontaminated benchmark

question_bank.rationale: The lecture lists corrupted data, bugs, and vanishing or exploding gradients as possible explanations for ugly or jumpy loss curves.

distractor_rationales.B: A balanced router would be a positive MoE signal, not the meaning of a loss jump.
distractor_rationales.C: CAMs are visual attribution methods, not loss-curve diagnostics.
distractor_rationales.D: Benchmark cleanliness is tested through contamination checks, not sudden training-loss jumps.

source_ref.evidence_span: You might find sudden jumps on the loss.

frame_evidence.description: Slide displays loss curves as a training-health diagnostic and examples of ugly or jumpy curves.

question_bank.stem: Beyond loss curves, which telemetry signal does the lecture explicitly name as part of the training dashboard?

options.text: Learning-rate schedule tracking
Occlusion-square size tracking
Reward-model preference ranking
Class-activation-map weighting

question_bank.rationale: The instructor mentions the learning-rate schedule as one training diagnostic signal after discussing loss curves and gradient problems.

distractor_rationales.B: Occlusion-square size is from CNN occlusion sensitivity, not frontier training telemetry.
distractor_rationales.C: Reward-model ranking belongs to RLHF, not this telemetry point.
distractor_rationales.D: CAM weighting is CNN localization, not training dashboard telemetry.

source_ref.evidence_span: look at your learning rate schedule,

question_bank.stem: Scaling laws are useful for model trainers because they relate performance to what tradeoff?

options.text: Model size, compute, and data size
Pixel brightness, occlusion size, and class label
Prompt length, temperature, and reward-model rank
Router name, expert color, and dashboard layout

question_bank.rationale: The lecture describes scaling laws as relationships between performance and hyperparameters such as model capacity, compute, and dataset size.

distractor_rationales.B: These variables belong to CNN/image attribution, not scaling laws.
distractor_rationales.C: These variables are not the compute-data-capacity tradeoff discussed here.
distractor_rationales.D: MoE router dashboards are separate from scaling-law variables.

source_ref.evidence_span: the model, the amount of compute that's being used

frame_evidence.description: Slide presents Chinchilla/scaling-law plots relating performance to compute, model size, and data.

question_bank.stem: The Chinchilla example supports which diagnosis of GPT-3-style training?

options.text: A smaller model trained more compute-optimally can outperform a larger undertrained model
A larger model always outperforms a smaller model regardless of data and compute
A model's benchmark score is valid even when test data is contaminated
A convolutional class activation map can replace scaling-law analysis

question_bank.rationale: The lecture says Chinchilla had fewer parameters than GPT-3 but performed better, illustrating undertraining and the importance of compute-optimal scaling.

distractor_rationales.B: The example is specifically used to reject this simple larger-is-always-better view.
distractor_rationales.C: Benchmark contamination is a separate caution in the next segment.
distractor_rationales.D: CAM is a CNN localization method, not a scaling-law substitute.

frame_evidence.description: Slide presents Chinchilla/scaling-law plots relating performance to compute, model size, and data.
